unit: Ch 1: Introduction to Cost and Management Accounting
note: AI-written summary of ICAI study material. Check the original for exact wording.

topics.title: Basic Definitions and Terminology
explain: Cost is the amount of resource given up, actual or notional, for goods or services.
Costing is the technique and process of ascertaining costs.
Cost Accounting records income and expenditure to ascertain and control costs.
Cost Accountancy applies costing and cost accounting principles, methods, and techniques to practice.
Management Accounting applies accounting principles to assist management in planning and decision making.
Cost Management applies management concepts to plan, monitor, and control organizational costs.
topics.example: Spending ₹100 on raw materials creates a cost; calculating per-unit expense is costing.
remember: Cost is both a noun (expenditure incurred) and a verb (action to ascertain cost).
mistakes: Confusing Costing (the process of ascertainment) with Cost Accounting (the formal recording process).

quiz.q: What is defined as the technique and process of ascertaining costs?
quiz.why: Costing is defined specifically as the technique and process of ascertaining costs.

quiz.q: Which term covers the application of costing and cost accounting principles to managerial decision making?
quiz.why: Cost Accountancy includes the science, art, and practice of cost control and profitability presentation.

topics.title: Objectives of Cost Accounting: Cost Control vs Cost Reduction
explain: Primary objectives include cost ascertainment, selling price fixation, cost control, cost reduction, and managerial assistance.
Cost control aims to maintain costs in accordance with established target standards.
Cost reduction achieves real and permanent unit cost reduction without impairing quality or suitability.
Cost control is a preventive function that ends when targets are achieved.
Cost reduction is a continuous corrective function that recognizes no condition as permanent.
topics.example: Keeping factory electricity use within budget is cost control; replacing bulbs with solar panels permanently is cost reduction.
remember: Cost reduction assumes permanent savings without degrading product quality or utility.
mistakes: Believing cost control continues indefinitely; cost control ends when target standards are met.

quiz.q: Which process is a continuous corrective function that assumes no cost condition is permanent?
quiz.why: Cost reduction continuously challenges standards to permanently lower unit costs without sacrificing quality.

quiz.q: What is the third step in the process of exercising cost control?
o: Comparison of actual performance with target
quiz.why: The sequence is: (1) set standard, (2) measure actuals, (3) compare, and (4) analyze variances.

topics.title: Scope, Functions, and Users of Cost Accounting
explain: Scope includes costing, cost accounting, cost analysis, comparisons, control, reports, and statutory compliances.
Functions focus on collecting, assigning, controlling costs, and feeding Management Information Systems (MIS).
Internal users include policy makers, managers, operational level staff, and employees.
External users include regulatory authorities, auditors, shareholders, creditors, and lenders.
topics.example: A production supervisor (internal user) checks idle time reports, while a lending bank (external user) checks stock statements.
remember: Shareholders and creditors are external users of cost accounting information.
mistakes: Classifying supervisors and operational team leaders as external users instead of internal users.

quiz.q: Which of the following is classified as an external user of cost and management accounting information?
quiz.why: Regulatory authorities are external bodies that inspect cost data for tariff or subsidy determinations.

quiz.q: What is the ultimate function in the scope of cost accounting?
quiz.why: Preparing Cost Reports for management decision-making is considered the ultimate function of cost accounting.

topics.title: Relationship of Cost Accounting with Other Disciplines
explain: Cost accounting records quantitative cost data for price fixation and cost control.
Financial accounting records monetary transactions to report overall financial performance of an entity.
Management accounting uses cost and financial accounting inputs to make future-oriented decisions.
Cost and Management Accounting applies financial management principles for operational decision making.
topics.example: Financial accounts show total company profit; cost accounts break down profit product by product.
remember: Cost accounting uses both historical and pre-determined data, whereas financial accounting uses historical data.
mistakes: Thinking cost accounting must follow rigid statutory formats like financial accounting statements.

quiz.q: Unlike Financial Accounting, Cost Accounting data consists of:
quiz.why: Cost accounting utilizes both historical costs and pre-determined (standard) costs for control.

quiz.q: Which accounting discipline deals with both qualitative and quantitative aspects for internal planning?
quiz.why: Management accounting records both qualitative and quantitative information for decision-making.

topics.title: Essentials and Installation of a Cost Accounting System
explain: A good costing system must be simple, informative, accurate, uniform, integrated, flexible, and trusted.
Before installation, an entity must evaluate its specific objectives and industry characteristics.
System design requires thorough knowledge of production processes, product types, and organizational structure.
Cost accounts must synchronize with financial accounts using control or integrated accounts.

flow.title: Installation Steps for a Costing System

topics.example: An oil refinery installs process costing to track crude oil stages, rather than job costing.
remember: A costing system should be tailor-made to the business without introducing unnecessary details.
mistakes: Attempting to set up a costing system without understanding the physical production process.

quiz.q: Which essential feature ensures comparability of cost reports across different time periods?
quiz.why: Uniformity and consistency in classification and treatment are essential for benchmarking and comparison.

quiz.q: Which factor must be studied first before setting up a cost accounting system?
quiz.why: The specific objective (e.g., price fixation vs. cost control) determines the initial system design.

topics.title: IT in Cost Accounting and Digital Costing Systems
explain: ERP integration allows single-entry data input to generate custom cost reports automatically.
IT moves organizations toward paperless operations using electronic requisitions and store notes.
Digital Costing under Industry 4.0 uses AI, Machine Learning, and Big Data for real-time tracking.
It links business functions with suppliers and market prices using Marked to Market (M2M) standards.
topics.example: Using an automated extranet system to trigger Just-In-Time (JIT) supplier orders without paper requisitions.
remember: Digital costing utilizes Marked to Market (M2M) pricing for raw materials and consumables.
mistakes: Confusing traditional batch ERP reporting with real-time AI/ML powered Digital Costing.

quiz.q: Digital Costing Systems use which mechanism to evaluate material costs on a real-time current market basis?
quiz.why: Digital costing leverages real-time data to estimate costs and set standards on a Marked to Market (M2M) basis.

quiz.q: How does IT integration reduce accounting effort when reconciling financial and cost records?
o: By single entry creating unified custom reports
quiz.why: ERPs integrate functional activities so a single data entry creates reports for both systems automatically.

topics.title: Cost Objects, Cost Units, and Cost Drivers
explain: Cost Object is any item, activity, department, or project for which separate cost measurement is required.
Cost Unit is a unit of quantity, service, or time in relation to which costs are expressed.
Cost Driver is a factor or activity responsible for causing or influencing cost incurrence.
Example cost units include kWh (power), passenger-kilometer (transport), and patient-day (hospitals).
topics.example: For a transport service (cost object), cost unit is passenger-km, and cost driver is distance traveled.
remember: A cost driver is the factor that directly links resource consumption to product outputs.
mistakes: Confusing Cost Unit (e.g., tonne of steel) with Cost Object (e.g., the steel plant or project).

quiz.q: What is the appropriate cost unit for a hospital industry sector according to CIMA terminology?
quiz.why: In hospital costing, costs are customarily measured and expressed per patient day.

quiz.q: Any activity or factor responsible for the incurrence of cost is called a:
quiz.why: A Cost Driver is defined as a factor or variable that influences or drives the level of cost.

topics.title: Responsibility Centres
explain: Responsibility Centres are organizational units whose managers are accountable for specified performance.
Cost Centres are accountable for costs. Standard Cost Centres have measurable output; Discretionary Cost Centres do not.
Revenue Centres are accountable for revenue generation (e.g., Sales Department).
Profit Centres are accountable for both revenues and costs (e.g., autonomous branch).
Investment Centres are accountable for profits and capital investment decisions (measured by ROI).
topics.example: R&D is a discretionary cost centre; a retail branch is a profit centre; PSU corporate headquarters is an investment centre.
remember: Standard cost centres have a clear input-output ratio, whereas discretionary cost centres do not.
mistakes: Assuming a sales counter is a profit centre when it has no control over product costs or capital.

quiz.q: Which type of cost centre has an output that cannot be measured in financial terms?
quiz.why: Discretionary cost centres (e.g., R&D or legal departments) produce outputs not directly measurable in financial terms.

quiz.q: A ticket counter in a Railway Station is an example of a:
quiz.why: A railway ticket counter is accountable specifically for sales revenue collection, making it a Revenue Centre.

topics.title: Limitations of Cost Accounting
explain: Expensive: Requires additional money and clerical work for overhead allocation and absorption.
Reconciliation Needed: Results shown by cost accounts often differ from financial accounts.
Duplication of Work: Entities maintain dual sets of accounts unless an integrated system is used.
topics.example: Preparing year-end reconciliation statements to explain profit differences between cost and financial books.
remember: Integrated accounting systems eliminate duplication by maintaining a single unified set of books.
mistakes: Believing cost accounting completely eliminates the statutory requirement for financial accounting.

quiz.q: Why is cost accounting considered expensive to operate?
o: Overhead analysis and allocation require additional work and money
quiz.why: Analysis, allocation, and absorption of overheads demand significant clerical work and extra costs.

quiz.q: What process is necessary when cost and financial accounts are maintained separately?
quiz.why: Reconciliation statements are required to explain profit discrepancies between dual account sets.

topics.title: Classification of Costs: Nature, Function, Controllability, Normality
explain: By Nature/Element: Material, Labour, and Other Expenses, subdivided into Direct and Indirect (Overheads).
By Function: Production, Administration, Selling, Distribution, and Research & Development costs.
By Controllability: Controllable costs can be influenced by a manager; Uncontrollable costs cannot.
By Normality: Normal costs are standard expected expenses; Abnormal costs are unexpected and charged to Costing P&L.

flow.title: Functional Cost Structure Flow
steps: Add Admin Overheads = Cost of Goods Sold
Add Selling & Distribution = Cost of Sales

topics.example: Material wasted due to a major plant fire is an abnormal cost debited to Costing Profit & Loss.
remember: Abnormal costs are never added to unit product cost; they go straight to Costing P&L.
mistakes: Classifying Administrative Overheads as part of Prime Cost.

quiz.q: Which of the following cost items is directly charged to the Costing Profit and Loss Account?
quiz.why: Abnormal costs are unexpected losses and are charged directly to Costing P&L.

quiz.q: Administrative Overheads are an example of cost classification by:
quiz.why: Classification into Production, Administration, Selling, and Distribution is based on functions.

topics.title: Cost Variability and Segregation of Semi-Variable Costs
explain: Fixed Costs remain constant in total across activity levels within specified output limits.
Variable Costs vary directly in total with changes in production volume.
Semi-variable Costs contain both fixed and variable elements (e.g., power bills).
Segregation methods: Graphical, High-Low, Analytical, Comparison by period/activity, and Least Squares.

flow.title: High-Low Segregation Steps
steps: Identify High and Low Activity Levels
Find Difference in Cost and Volume
Divide Cost Change by Volume Change
Deduct Total Variable Cost to find Fixed Cost

topics.example: A taxi charging ₹80 flat minimum plus ₹12 per kilometer represents a semi-variable cost.
remember: Variable Cost per Unit = (Change in Total Expense) / (Change in Output Quantity).
mistakes: Assuming fixed cost per unit remains constant when production output fluctuates.

quiz.q: If total semi-variable cost is ₹300 for 100 units and ₹340 for 140 units, what is the variable cost per unit?
quiz.why: Change in cost = ₹40 (340-300); Change in units = 40 (140-100); Variable rate = ₹40/40 = ₹1 per unit.

quiz.q: Which method uses the linear equation y = mx + c to split semi-variable costs?
quiz.why: The Least Square Method is a statistical method using the linear equation y = mx + c.

topics.title: Costs Used in Managerial Decision Making
explain: Pre-determined / Standard Costs are computed in advance based on expected efficient operations.
Marginal Cost is the change in total cost resulting from producing one additional unit.
Differential Cost represents the change in total cost between two alternatives.
Opportunity Cost is the value of benefit foregone by choosing one alternative over another.
Sunk Costs are historical past costs irrelevant to future managerial decisions.
Imputed Costs are notional cash-free costs, while Out-of-pocket Costs require actual cash outlays.

flow.title: Decision-Making Cost Analysis
steps: Select Option with Highest Net Benefit

topics.example: Interest lost by using company bank savings to purchase new machines is an opportunity cost.
remember: Sunk costs (such as written-down asset values) must be ignored in future decision evaluations.
mistakes: Including notional/imputed costs as cash expenses in financial accounting ledger books.

quiz.q: Historical costs incurred in the past that are irrelevant to current decision making are known as:
quiz.why: Sunk costs are past historical expenses that cannot be changed and must be ignored in decisions.

quiz.q: Costs that involve immediate outlay of cash funds are termed as:
quiz.why: Out-of-pocket costs (or explicit costs) require direct, immediate cash outflows.

topics.title: Methods of Costing
explain: Single / Output Costing: Used when a single uniform product is produced (e.g., bricks, coal).
Batch Costing: Applied when identical products are produced in batches (e.g., medicines, spare parts).
Job Costing: Used for customized work executed per customer specifications (e.g., printing press).
Contract Costing: Applied to long-term major construction contracts (e.g., bridges, buildings).
Process / Operation Costing: Applied when goods pass through continuous sequential processes (e.g., sugar, chemicals).
Operating Costing: Used by service-rendering entities (e.g., transport, hospitals, hotels).
Multiple Costing: Combination of two or more costing methods (e.g., automobile assembly).
topics.example: A pharmaceutical firm uses batch costing for medicine tablets, while a printer uses job costing.
remember: Multiple costing combines various methods (like batch and single costing) for complex goods like cars.
mistakes: Applying job costing to continuous mass production of identical chemical items.

quiz.q: Which costing method is most suitable for chemical manufacturing industries?
quiz.why: Chemical industries process raw materials in continuous sequential stages, making Process Costing suitable.

quiz.q: Car assembly units manufacturing complex multi-component products use:
quiz.why: Multiple costing is applied when different component parts require various costing methods before final assembly.

topics.title: Techniques of Costing
explain: Uniform Costing: Common costing principles adopted by multiple firms in an industry for comparison.
Marginal Costing: Ascertains cost by separating fixed and variable costs to evaluate profit-volume impact.
Standard Costing: Compares pre-determined target standard costs with actual costs for variance control.
Historical Costing: Ascertains costs after they have been incurred (Post Costing or Continuous Costing).
Absorption Costing: Assigns both fixed and variable manufacturing costs to output products.
topics.example: Comparing actual monthly raw material spending against standard pre-set allowances is standard costing.
remember: Absorption costing includes fixed costs in product unit cost, whereas marginal costing excludes fixed costs.
mistakes: Confusing Costing Methods (how cost is collected, like Job/Process) with Costing Techniques (how cost is analyzed, like Marginal/Standard).

quiz.q: Which costing technique charges both variable and fixed costs to operations or products?
quiz.why: Absorption Costing is the practice of charging all costs (both variable and fixed) to products.

quiz.q: What is the primary feature of Uniform Costing?
o: Adopting the same costing system across multiple firms
Excluding fixed costs from product cost
Calculating variances on real-time AI networks
quiz.why: Uniform costing occurs when multiple firms agree to follow identical costing rules for inter-firm comparison.
